speechtext:
I quite realize the circumstances under which this amendment is being introduced, but I question whether it is not going too far in placing the onus upon the accused. The principle of common law is, of course, that the onus must always rest upon the crown. The amendment reads as follows:
. . . any person who while intoxicated or under the influence of any narcotic occupies the seat ordinarily occupied by a person driving a motor vehicle shall be deemed to have the care and control of the said motor vehicle unless the said person establishes that he did not enter or mount the said vehicle for the purpose of setting it in motion.
I can appreciate the reason for the amendment, because certain judges have held that a person sitting behind the wheel of a car that is not in motion is not driving that car, nor has he any control over it. I rise only for the pui-pose of pointing out that in accepting this departure from the major principle of criminal law, namely that the onus rests upon the crown, I hope the minister does not take it as a precedent to remove that safeguard, which is of the essence of British criminal law, as far as other sections are concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext: When I have more time I want to give the house the long list of sections in the criminal code where the onus is shifted in circumstances something like these, and to point out that if this were not the case, law enforcement would be impossible. I realize the validity of the underlying general principle, and that it should not be interfered with except in the case of necessity, and, generally speaking, where the means of proof are peculiarly with the defendant.

subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext: In the knowledge of the defendant.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS

speechtext:
Does the minister not think perhaps this amendment will encourage a drunken driver to keep on driving in an endeavour to get home? It seems to me that if a man is driving a car and realizes that he is drunk the proper thing for him to do is to pull over to the side of the road and sleep it off instead of trying to get home. It seems

Criminal Code
to me that, under this amendment, once a man has started to drive while in that condition, he is guilty of this offence, and, knowing that,, he will try to carry on until he gets home, whereas what he should do when he finds he cannot handle the car is to get to the side of the road and sleep it off.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS

subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS

subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I wonder why the minister does not include the driver of a motor boat in this section. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS

subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext: That has happened at many places throughout the country, and I do not think there is any law to protect those in other boats. subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Suppose this motor boat driver realizes he is drunk; what should he do? He cannot park on the side of the road. Should he jump in the lake?

subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Notwithstanding the heavy loss of life, we have yet to provide a section dealing adequately with this offence. As the chief analyst for the Ontario government has said, eighty per cent of the accidents on our highways are caused by people who are not fit to drive their cars because of the intoxicants they have taken. It is all very well to talk about those who are in charge of a ear. Some people sleep in their cars. Recently in my own city they have moved all the cars off the downtown streets and put them on the waterfront. Others sleep in trailers, which the-y are trying to move now to make room for the sick children's hospital. This section has not been strengthened at all. The proposed amendment will cause far more confusion .than there has been under the existing law. The appalling fatal accidents and injuries from highway motor traffic are mounting steadily night and day. Every highway in Canada is coloured red with the slaughter. The loss in men, women and children, as well as the economic loss, is deplorable.
Several months ago, when I proposed an amendment, somewhat similar to this one the minister showed a great deal of sympathy. Many of these accidents are caused by failure to exercise care and judgment, on the part of those who drive these deadly, menacing machines. Nothing has contributed so much as the motor car to the education and enjoyment of the public. But, like every other great invention, and as in connection with medicine, science, physics and chemistry, use is one thing and abuse is another. Because of the abuse of the motor car in Canada today, we read in our newspapers every day about these casualties. On Dominion day, Tuesday of this week, there were seventy-five casualties, some of which were from drowning, but the great majority from the use of motor cars.
I hope that something may be done under this provision to remove this public scandal. Every highwa3' is coloured, red with slaughter, and nothing has been done, so far as I can see in this section, to cure the disease. The total list of those killed and injured on the highways of England, the United States and Canada during the six years of the war was almost equal to the number of casualties of those killed and injured in the war.
I have referred to this matter on many occasions, and I shall not occupy more of the time of the committee this evening. I do not say anything by way of criticism of the minister or of his deputy, because the minister has indeed a most able deputy at the present time, a man who has the advantage of having come from Toronto. The deputy minister of justice, Mr. Varcoe, K.C., C.M.G., was educated at Harbord collegiate, which has produced some great men, including Sir Edward Beatty, Beverley Baxter, Garfield Weston and others.
I call to the minister's attention the recommendations of chief justices, judges and magistrates and the law courts, the bar association. the chief constables' association and others for the cure of this disease. I doubt very much that the changing of a few words here and there will obtain the object the minister has in mind, because anyone can say now, "I did not intend to drive the car, no matter where I was sitting'', and he will get the benefit of the doubt.

I should like the minister to tell us in what way he thinks he is strengthening the section, or in what way it is better than the original one. It states:
(4) Everyone who, while intoxicated or under the influence of any narcotic, drives any motor vehicle or automobile, or has the care or control of a motor vehicle or automobile, whether it is in motion or not, shall be guilty of an offence.
Surely that section is as clear as it can be. If the accused person has the care or control he is guilty, whether it is in motion or not. I know a court has decided that if it was not in motion and the man was drunk there was nothing to show that he had it under his control.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Right.

subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext: But I cannot see how we have made it any stronger by this amendment. The way it is now, the only difference it makes is that the onus is thrown upon a man, and it must have been on him before.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext: He was guilty if he was sitting in the car.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext: In the amendment the only difference is that he can get up and say that he did not enter the vehicle to set it in motion. He may have had it in motion, and may have stopped a moment. He may have been under the influence, but if he says he did not mount it for the purpose of starting it he is free. It should be stronger than that., if we are ever to get a court to make a conviction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
The only way to make it stronger is to leave out the concluding words, "unless the said person establishes that he did not enter or mount the said vehicle for the purpose of setting it in motion." If we leave off those words we expose a person who accidentally, in a drunken stupor, gets into a car to go to sleep, or something of that kind. He is left open to a conviction. That person never did have the control of the car, and he should be given an opportunity of showing that he did not enter the car or get on the motorcycle, if a motorcycle is involved, for the purpose of setting it in motion, and that he was not in the car for that purpose at all. That should be a defence to such a person.
But if those words are left off everyone would be subject to conviction.

subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Those words were not in the old act. If he was in it, whether it was in motion or not, he was supposed to be guilty of the offence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext: No, with deference, I think the hon. member is wrong. Before this amendment, if his state of intoxication were sufficiently advanced the courts in many of the provinces held he did not have control of the motor vehicle. It is no longer open to an accused person to defend himself on those grounds. The early words in this proviso take that defence away from him. But they leave a defence to a person who, having got into the car for the purpose of setting it in motion, goes to sleep.

subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext: It takes away a defence that was not very strong and gives him a defence that is strong.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS

I return to the point I tried to make a moment ago. It seems to me that a man who is drunk and stops his car on the side of the road for the same purpose, namely to sleep it off, should be in just as strong a position as the drunken man who got into the car, not intending to start off with it. The other man got into the car with the intention of driving it. He does drive it for a distance and finds he is incapable of doing so. Therefore he wisely drives off to the side of the road. I say he should be protected just as much as the drunken man who gets in but does not start the car at all.
Mr. ILSLEY': The hon. member's argument leads to this conclusion, that we should not change the section at all. Perhaps we should not. But certainly we have been severely criticized by the courts for not changing it. There is a recent judgment of a judge in the supreme court of New Brunswick which is most caustic in its reference to the lawmakers. The reason is obvious.
If persons accused of driving a car while intoxicated can go into a court and say, "I was too drunk to be guilty," it shocks the public; indeed it shocks us all, I believe.

subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I hold no brief for the drunken driver; I hate him. I do not like defending them, either in court or in parliament, But I believe that if we are giving a break to the man who gets in and does not start the car, the man who uses his head and, when he finds he is drunk, is wise enough to stop, should be protected possibly more than the other chap.

subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I am going to suggest that the words which have been used to indicate that the man entered the automobile be changed. It does not seem to me that it makes much difference what his purpose was on entering the automobile, so long as he

Criminal Code
was in it without the intention of setting it in motion. The words now are:
Provided that any person who while intoxicated or under the influence of any narcotic occupies the seat ordinarily occupied by a person driving a motor vehicle shall be deemed to have the care or control of the said motor vehicle unless the said person establishes that he did not enter or mount the said vehicle.
If the words "enter or mount" were changed to the words, "unless he establish that he was not in the said vehicle" he would then be in the position in which I think the minister wants him to be. It would enable a person to show that, having entered an automobile with the intention of setting it in motion, he had not done so, or, having done so, had ceased to keep it in motion. I would think that change would enable the person to set up a defence which might exculpate him in circumstances where he would necessarily be condemned if he had entered the car with the intention of setting it in motion, whether he did or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
It may logically be so,
but would it not really mean that the section would become unenforceable. An accused person could step up and swear, "It is true I was in the car; it is true I was behind the wheel; it is true I was driving the car, or I entered it with the intention of driving it, but there came a time when I did not intend to drive it any more. I was drunk behind the wheel of the car; I had been driving it, but I stopped driving it and I did not intend to start the car again." I do not think he should get off under those circumstances.

subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Nor do I. If he said
that he would be guilty.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Not under the amendment
suggested by the hon. gentleman. His suggestion is that the section be amended so that it will read, "unless the said person establishes that he is not in the said vehicle for the purpose of setting it in motion." That would enable him to say, "True, I got in for that purpose and I drove it; I was drunk at the time and drunk before I got in, but there came a time when I decided not to drive it any more. I am testifying to that; nobody can deny that was my state of mind and, therefore, I am not guilty." That man ought to be held to be guilty.

subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I am not going to carry
the argument much farther, but I do not think my suggestion lends itself to that interpretation. If a man were driving a oar I do not think it would be open to him to say that it was not his intention to do so. What I am endeavouring to do is to protect the person 83166-323
who, having entered a car with the intention of driving it, was not driving it, in that it was still at the moment of the collision or whatever happened.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman suggesting that he never drove it, that he entered the car and did not drive it at any time?

subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
He may have driven it,
but he had ceased to drive it. As I interpret this amendment, it merely means that the man having entered the vehicle for the purpose of setting it in motion, a situation is created from which he cannot escape. My suggestion is that, having entered it with the intention of setting it in motion, if he ceases to keep it in motion, then he may escape.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I think that is a bit fine
spun to incorporate into legislation. If a man is drunk and gets in a car, while he is behind the wheel of that car I think he comes within the spirit of the original section which was that he should be convicted if he had the care and control of the car while intoxicated. It should not be open to him to say, "I was too drunk to be said to have the car under my control even though I was sitting behind the wheel." It should not be open to him to be able to say that.

subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
My suggestion was not
that he be able to avail himself of the suggestion set forth by the minister.

subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Is there any other section in the criminal code under which a man may be convicted of an offence when, under the statute, he is guilty only of the intention to commit an offence? That is what this amendment does. If a man gets in a car and intends to drive it and does not drive it, under this amendment he is guilty of an offence although he is guilty actually of only the intention to commit an offence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext: He is not to be convicted of intent only; he is being convicted of intent plus the act. The act is taking custody of a car, being in the car, having the car under his care and control while he is drunk, plus the intent of setting the car in motion after he got into it.

subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
The explanatory note to this section states that the amendment is made following recent court decisions to the effect that a driver may be too drunk to have the care or control of a motor vehicle. There is a great need for a drastic revision of this particular section which is amending subsection 4 of section 285, as enacted by section

Criminal Code

6 of chapter 11 of the statutes of 1930. Professor Jocelyn Rodgers, medico-legal expert of Ontario and of the attorney general's department, a gentleman who has been giving evidence all over the province in connection with this section, says it is not the drunken driver who is the greatest menace-he is, as a rule, quite harmless-it is the man who drives in a state of slight conviviality with enough alcohol to give him a little exhilarated feeling and inspires him to take a chance at a time when that amount of alcohol will slow down the action of his brain and nerve cells so that when a crisis arises he cannot act quickly.
The railroads have a rule, known as rule G, which forbids any employee to touch alcoholic beverages while on duty. That rule states that a man driving a railroad engine should have no alcohol in his system. . Whether these institutions are rightly or wrongly managed, the fact is that they are managed by crown officers, and the public

The principle of
nolle prosequi is that the attorney general of a province may determine that there is no evidence upon which a conviction can be registered, or he may conclude that a man has already been sufficiently punished for the offence committed. For instance, it arises quite frequently that a. man is charged with three different thefts. He is sentenced on those thefts and,' later on, a fourth theft arises. Instead of having that person again go through the mill of a trial the attorney general may direct the crown prosecutor or the crown attorney to return a nolle prosequi."

Under those circumstances the prosecution would not be proceeded with. In that principle there is no lack of uniformity. That principle dates back to the time of habeas corpus when, for the first time, the crown vested in its servants the right to direct that in the interests of justice prosecution ought not to take place. But this is a departure which I view with considerable alarm. It places the human factor foremost in the determination of whether or not a person shall be proceeded against.

The first object of criminal law is the protection of society and this seems to be necessary for the protection of society. My hon. friend says that it will induce a lack of uniformity in the law; he referred to the law of England and undertook to show that the right of the attorney general to direct that no prosecutions take place is there and has been carried into the law of Canada and attorneys general have the right to call off prosecutions. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
That is not our system in Canada. Nothing is more fundamental in our system than the administration of justice and the enforcement of law are the responsibility of the provinces, not of the Attorney General of Canada, but of the attorney general of each province. In England they have passed similar legislation providing that no charge of being an habitual criminal shall be inserted in an indictment without the consent of the director of public prosecutions. They put that in, because it is a serious thing to charge a person with being an habitual criminal, leading a persistently criminal life. They wanted to make it clear that he did not have to be charged with that in every instance, and so they said that the consent of the director of public prosecutions would be required. We are putting in the same provision hare in Canada and substituting the only officials we can substitute under our constitution, and that is the attorney general of the province for the director of general prosecutions. That is not peculiar to this act at all. It is worth while to put on record some of the sections where the same principle applies. 1 will give the numbers of the sections first: Sections 205A,
592, 594, 596, 597, 598, 777 and 825. These relate to various offences with which persons cannot be charged without the leave of the attorney general of the province and, in some cases, the Attorney General of Canada where the matter has some peculiar connection with dominion jurisdiction. Section 205A deals with parading while nude, and so on, and the section concludes with these words:
No action or prosecution for a violation of this section shall be commenced without the leave of the attorney general for the province in which the offence is alleged to have been committed.
Section 592 relates to the offence of disclosing official secrets and provides that no person shall be prosecuted for that offence without the consent of the attorney general of the province or of the Attorney General of Canada. Section 593 makes necessary the leave of the Attorney General of Canada. Section 594 deals with explosive substances and there can be no prosecution without the consent of the attorney general. Section 596 deals with criminal breach of trust-no prosecution without the consent of the attorney general. Similarly for the other sections I have mentioned. So there is a class of offences where no proceedings can be taken without the consent of the attorney general. It is the attorney general who prefers the indictment through his officer, the crown prosecutor. This makes it clear that he is not obliged in every case to prefer this charge. I do not see how you could have it any other way.

speechtext: I wanted to support the hon. member for Lake Centre in his plea to the minister, but the minister has already given his answer. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITION OF PART DEALING WITH HABITUAL CRIMINALS-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
The Attorney General of Canada comes in where the matter is one in which the dominion has definite concern. Section 593, for example, provides:
No one holding any judicial office shall be prosecuted for the offence of judicial corruption, without the leave of the Attorney General of Canada.
It is the government of Canada that appoints the judges. That is tied up to the dominion. But the ordinary, prosecution of criminals is a provincial matter, and I 9o not think it would be proper for the dominion government to endeavour to project itself
Criminal Code
into that field by trying to say what charges should be laid by provincial attorneys general and what should not, because that is what it would amount to.

I would suggest to the minister that the criminal code provides for a penitentiary system which is under the jurisdiction of the dominion and that the man who would be tried for being a habitual criminal will have spent at least one or two terms in the penitentiary. Therefore the federal department would be much better able to judge whether that man should be tried as a habitual criminal, because it would have the information from the superintendent of the penitentiary and the penitentiary officials as to just what sort of person the man was.

I do not rise to discuss this clause in a spirit of criticism. It is perhaps due to some mechanism in me that I cannot conceive or understand how we can incarcerate anybody by anticipation. I know it is the principle of magna carta that no man shall be held in prison without having previously been judged by his peers. That is an established principle we were all brought up to respect and to follow. And if I were met with the answer that the man had been judged because he had committed three offences and that is why he should be incarcerated for an indefinite period-that is something I just cannot assimilate. It makes me think of the poem of Alexander Pope who said: "It is a question whether want of skill appears in writing or in judging ill." By what measure of psychological conception, by what interpretation of law, by what system of calculation can we arrive at the conclusion that, because a man has committed an offence three times, he is therefore a habitual criminal and whether, with the consent or without the consent of the attorney general, he can be put away, subject to revision which will always confirm the reports of the superintendent of the penitentiary? I am wondering whether we are not committing a crime against criminals.
I have seen hon. members sitting on this side of the fence; I have seen a man psychologically, perhaps by a perverted mentality, by a sadistic attitude who will say, "come on; let us put him away." Society admits that it can do nothing with its offenders; that it cannot reform them; that it cannot redeem them; that it has gone bankrupt in social conduct and that we want to put a man away because we anticipate he is going to commit a crime. You say to him, Well, this man has been condemned three times. This is an importation into Canada. I do not IMr. Ilsley.]
want any precedents cited from the state of Michigan which condemns a man probably to life for having committed three small crimes. I do not want to play with the gastric juices of any judge who some morning may have an attack of indigestion and say, "I am going to put away this fellow." The word "judge" does not scare me. Judges are not infallible. Even God Almighty does not want to destroy the sinner. All He wants is for him to redeem himself. Here we are smarter than God Almighty. We are going to do something that God would not do. I want to know by what standard of measurement, by what norm we come to the conclusion. I know that some psychologists, some psychoanalysts, some of those who probe the minds and souls of men have something to say about such treatment. Personally I think they know nothing at all about it, because if they were psychoanalyzed in turn it would be found that it was too soon to let them out and too late to let them in.
I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that I do not understand by what principle this is being done. Is it because some men want to show their usefulness? I?p to the seventeenth century there were 175 crimes punishable by death in England, which did not deter crime. It has been going on. I remember reading of a case where a man witnessed the hanging in Virginia of a man who had picked the pocket of somebody. While he was witnessing the hanging, he was picking the pocket of somebody else. Did that stop the habitual criminal?
I do not want to compare the legislators of this house to the dictators of Europe who, being personally corrupted and perverted, infused their attitude into the administration of their respective governments and put people in concentration camps under the pretext that it was protective custody.
And gassed them.

Gassed them and made soap out of them. It was a paying proposition. They were doing it for the good of society.
I do not know of any law that is not introduced for the good of society. Canada has got along well for eighty years. We have a criminal code that is as rigid as can be. We have noted every crime that can be committed that is punishable on its own merits and by judging each incident. Why is it that we have to give this latitude of incarcerating men by anticipation. Who is to read their minds? Who is to take that responsibility? We are somewhat civilized. I said "somewhat".

Oftentimes we are far from being civilized.

I should like to agree with the hon. gentleman, but I must be very careful. The point that I am trying to make to the committee is, what caused the necessity?
Some hon. MEMBERS : Carried.

They have to remember that they are the elected representatives of the people. It may inadvertently strike the son of any man who is here, and then they will say, how foolish the law must have been.
What 1 object to, Mr. Chairman, is the principle of the thing, to condemn a man for an offence he has not committed. It is not British; it is not Canadian. We have never heard of such things. Who is to review the case? With all due respect to the deputy minister of justice-he may be a man of great knowledge-he cannot review all cases. Some junior comes into the Department of Justice. Hon. members ought to see some opinions handed out in the name of justice. I do not think there is a court in Canada which would uphold the-m,. but that would be the opinion and the man would remain incarcerated, We are cons'oled by the assurance of the Minister of Justice who, I know, is a fair man, an honest man, that the case will be reviewed every three years. What a splendid vacation, to put a man away on some subjective suspicion because he was condemned three times before. There are a lot of men who are not caught the third time and are still loose, and often these men are to go away for life. I ask the Minister of Justice to consider the matter. It is an Americanism we have imported. The state of Michigan has it. I think the state of New York has it; but it is a state law; it is not a federal law and does not apply to the whole of the United States. Here we are passing a law that is going into perpetuity, that because a man has committed a crime three times he ipso facto is condemned as a habitual criminal.
On this point I must agree with the hon. member for Lake Centre. We want to protect ourselves and excuse ourselves for our failure to reform these criminals. Whether it is psychological, or whatever it is, we have done nothing in Canada to reform the criminal.
Not of any consequence.

No, we have not done anything in Canada. For a prisoner to live in incarceration, society will consider that he has paid his penalty. In order to clear ourselves of that delicate consciousness of ours, we say we can do nothing, that the man is a habitual criminal. I hope that the Minister
of Justice will reflect on the matter. I am not here to teach him. I know he is a good lawyer; I know he knows the social conditions under which we live. I know there are some inadvertent moments in the playing around with this problem of attorneys general. I agree again with the hon. member for Lake Centre. I have my suspicions, because I do not know who are the gods and who are the devils. I do not know who is to judge advantageously to himself and who may play polities with a law such as this. We have heard of the principle of nolle prosequi. An hon. member was asked about the case of nolle prosequi. That is a thing they play with. In criminal law constitutionally it has become general. That is the constitution of Canada. Of course the attorneys general always have the discretion. Then they have to resort to nolle prosequi, no proof to proceed further. Those who practise law know very well what it means. I appeal to the Minister of Justice and to hon. members to reconsider the idea of putting a man in a concentration camp and to justify our action 'to say, "Now, you are a bad little boy; we are going to call you a habitual criminal" I think we are committing a crime against the criminals.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I just want to say that I believe the hon. member for Cartier is thinking too much about the criminal and too little about society for whose protection we have to pass these laws. I think that is the fallacy of his approach. The important thing, after all, is the protection of society, and I cannot work up very great feelings of righteous indignation in favour of the suggestion that we are unjust in this law to men who have been guilty of serious crimes three times, as shown by their convictions, and who have committed a fourth crime and have been found by judge and jury to be leading persistently criminal lives. That is what they are punished' for and not for any crime they have not committed. They are not punished in anticipation, but for what they have done, and this is a form of punishment which is necessary for the protection of society.
If a man is charged on three different counts and is found guilty on all three, that is only one conviction? It is the same crime.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, I think so.

My hon. friend has raised a point that is worth serious consideration, because the section reads:
A person shall not be found to be a habitual criminal unless the judge or jury as the case may be, finds on evidence,
Criminal Code

(a) that since attaining the age of eighteen years he has at least three times previously to the conviction of the crime charged in the indictment, been convicted of an indictable offence for which he was liable to at least five years' imprisonment . . .
-and also that he is leading a persistently criminal life. The hon. member has raised a point that is particularly sound. If a person were charged with theft, obtaining under false pretences, and a third offence within the same indictment, all of which were subject to punishment of at least five years' imprisonment, and if he were found guilty of all three he might very well come within these provisions.
Or even three counts of breaking in at night would be sufficient.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I take it to mean, different times.
It, does not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, that is what it states. I certainly intended, and I think the intention of the law is, that if he is charged in one indictment with several crimes, the convictions on that indictment are deemed to be at one time.
They may not be.
Could it not be stated, three different indictments and three separate convictions?
I have seen it happen that there were ten counts of breaking in-
On one indictment.

Yes. He pleaded guilty on four and not guilty on six. He was found guilty, later, on three, so that there were two convictions at different times on the same indictment, and it is possible that there might be three convictions on the same indictment at different times.
That would make a good point for appeal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I certainly intended that the convictions on one indictment should be deemed to be the one conviction at that time, so that you could not say he was convicted at different times simply because different convictions took place as a result of one indictment. I should think, if there were any doubt about the matter, the attorney general would proceed accordingly.

Another case that might be imagined is this. Suppose a person has lived a decent life and suddenly he begins to commit crimes. He commits three different

thefts in different parts of his province all wuthin a matter of a few days, and he is charged in point A, in point B and in point C and is convicted in each. You have three convictions and the man is a habitual criminal, unless some change is made here.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It must also be established that he is leading a persistently criminal life, and I should think that would be a case where he wmuld not, even be charged with it.
He would have to be found guilty of being a habitual criminal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

Is it intended that the person charged with being an habitual criminal shall have served a sentence on each of three different occasions; that is to say, that he shall have served three sentences for three different crimes before this would apply?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

Could it not be worded in that way, then, so that he would not be serving two or three sentences concurrently, but three separate sentences one after another? That is what the minister is trying to get at.
It says "convicted".

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The important thing is that he be convicted at successive times. The essence of the section, is that there be conviction at this particular time of his life, and a conviction again at another time, and a third conviction at still another time, and that it be established also that he is leading a persistently criminal life. That is the intention, and that is the way in which it should be viewed by the attorneys general who administer it. I think the intention is clear enough.
I believe that is what is meant, but legal opinion here seems to differ.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think it is clear.

I suggest 575C (a), at the top of page 7, might be looked at. After the word "imprisonment" there might be added the words "and has served three separate terms of imprisonment for such offences."
Mr. ILSLEY': The trouble there is that the sentence might be suspended. He might have been released on suspended sentence the first time, but that should not prevent him from being regarded as having committed a crime. That was a conviction, and I think that should be counted.	.

Section agreed to.
Sections 19 to 23 inclusive agreed to.
On section 24-'Appeal on ground involving question of law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is to be a slight change here. The word "that", the first word on line 22, must be deleted. It is really a clerical error.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
Sections 25 and 26 agreed to.
On section 27-Fees.

I should like to draw attention to the fact that in connection with summonses taken out by officers of the mounted police it has been the practice of the mounted police to serve these summonses themselves, even at distances as great as twenty miles and at places where there are bailiffs who could perform the service. The result is that the defendant has to pay large costs. I have seen one case in which the costs amounted to $18 for the service of the summons, whereas if it had been sent to a bailiff the cost would have been only fifty cents, because he lived less than a mile from the person served.
C'est le meme principe que dans un cas de procedure civile.

Yes. In our code of civil procedure in the province of Quebec we have a rule that the greatest amount which may be charged for the service of a summons or writ is the amount that may be charged by the bailiff living nearest the defendant. This provision in the code will create an injustice. It is not the same thing as the case of an arrest. As a matter of fact, in Quebec the department of the attorney general always used the services of bailiffs, and the officers of the provincial police or of the liquor commission do not serve these summonses. I think it is only fair that they should be served by bailiffs, and it would not require any change in the law; it would only require instructions to the Royal Canadian Mounted
Police. It is as simple as that, and it would correct an injustice which is contrary to the general practice in the province.
Does not the criminal code say the summons ha_s to be served by a constable?
No, it does not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will give consideration to the hon. gentleman's suggestion. I was not aware of the practice he mentions, and I do not think it can be extensive.
It is extensive. As far as I know, it is done in every case in the province of Quebec, and I have had many complaints.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I shall look into the matter and see whether my hon. friend's point can be met.

In the schedule the witness fee is fixed at $3. That is too much, if I may say so. In the west you may bring six or eight or ten witnesses in a small case, even one heard by a justice. If that is done in trials of small importance the costs are made too great. People cannot afford them; they will go to gaol instead of paying a fine and costs. In many of these small trials they have more witnesses than the courtroom can hold.

I think it is recognised that even these fees are subject to the discretion of the presiding judge or magistrate. One hon. member spoke of the excessive cost of having summonses served in certain districts. I believe the presiding magistrate or judge sees that these summonses are served in the most economical way possible, and police officers are not permitted to travel long distances and run up large costs. I know in my own experience the presiding magistrate or judge generally insists upon the most economical service being carried out. because if we run up heavy costs in court actions we shall do more harm than good. The minister might take that into consideration and see that the fees are only permissive, giving the magistrate or judge discretion in awarding them.

I would suggest that
there be a basic rate for service by constables. It does seem unfair that because a man lives twenty miles from the county town it should cost him more to be served. The offence is no greater than in the case of a man living in town. I should think that, by averaging the amount so that everyone would pay the same for service, we would get a fair method.

I should like to support that suggestion. In the west they have long
Criminal Code

distances to travel. Sometimes a man must be brought from thirty or forty miles away, and even farther in my own district. The costs of serving witnesses, with mileage and so on, become so burdensome the people simply cannot pay them.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Carried.
Can we not get an answer?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If there is anything wrong with this scale of fees we should not pass it. As I understand the objections that have been raised, they are, first, that the witness fee of $3 a day is too much, and, then, that the fees of the constables should be averaged in some way. Were there any other suggestions I did not hear? I believe those were the only two. At the moment I do not see how this averaging that has been suggested could be done. I believe this is the system followed everywhere.
Mr. BOL'CHER: I believe the minister understands the situation which is encountered more particularly in the rural districts, where they have long distances to travel. In this city, for example, costs are much higher in the county police court than in the city police court. In the city court they can serve individuals charged with various offences within a very short time, and the costs are reasonable. But take the case of an individual who has committed an offence, who lives some distance from the city and who has to be served with a process. If a policeman is sent out thirty or forty miles to bring in a witness one will find that the same two men, charged with exactly the same offence, will pay entirely different penalties for their offences. I say a gross injustice is being done, and having that disparity does not work to the benefit of proper law administration. If the minister could equalize it by having a flat rate I believe there would be a better administration of justice, and in the end it would be much better than the scale basis. Presiding judges or magistrates may have some discretion, but they do not always use it. One can realize that particularly in connection with offences where fines are imposed; and where the fines are going to one department of government or another, the magistrate must consider seriously the costs of serving processes as well as the collection of fines from the culprits. The accused person is often handicapped thereby.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not believe that I shall offer any amendment to this, because much consideration has been given to this matter of fees. I have been making some inquiries
tMr. Miller.]
from one hon. member who has had considerable experience in at least one province in respect of witness fees, and he informs me that there is considerable difficulty in having witnesses attend, at all, because the fees have been so low.

They claim it is not
sufficient.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I suppose the witnesses are obliged to come.
Bu't they complain about it.

Anyone who has had any experience in the administration of justice can assure the minister that, no matter what fees were paid to witnesses, they would not want to come. I do not think any witness will come to court simply because the fee is raised.

Section agreed to.
Sections 28 to 31 inclusive agreed to.
On section 32-Reduction of imprisonment on part payment of sum adjudged to be paid.

Is this not a vicious section, in that it seems to make the court a collection agency? A man receives a term of imprisonment for non-payment of a sum of money, and then he can pay part of it and, by so doing, receive a reduction in the number of days he must serve. Probably that is a benevolent thing to do, but it is hardily in accord with the manner in which we carry on British justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This amendment was recommended by the commissioners on the uniformity of legislation, and it seems fair. On what ground does the hon. member object?

In many cases matters are rushed to court because the damages are not taken care of. The result is that a conviction is registered and money is to be paid. This indicates that the force of law would' be used to force a man to pay.

This reduction of sentence when the accused has been convicted and is subject to fine and imprisonment applies only to the fine being paid to the crown. It does not apply to a remittance of money when a magistrate orders an accused person to make a remittance. An unjust situation arises when a man who has been convicted and is subject to fine or imprisonment does not happen to have enough money to pay all the fine. He has to go to gaol because he cannot pay the $100 he has been fined, when he has only $50 with which to wipe out half the term of imprisonment. I believe this provision is fair to the accused man.

Forest Conservation

That the words "that the said act be amended'' in the first fine of section 32 be stricken out and the words "the said act is further amended" be substituted therefor.

subtopic: EASTERN SLOPE OF ROCKY MOUNTAINS- AGREEMENT WITH ALEERTA

speechtext:
The house resumed from Tuesday, July 1, consideration in committee of Bill No. 362, respecting the protection and conservation of the forests on the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains-Mr. Howe-Mr. Macdonald (Bra-ntford City) in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.

subtopic: EASTERN SLOPE OF ROCKY MOUNTAINS- AGREEMENT WITH ALEERTA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, for perhaps half a dozen or more years I had the
pleasure of travelling over the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains, and at that time I became greatly alarmed at the lack of protection against fire and other things which might destroy the forests. I am rising to support this bill strongly for the second time. I appreciate that the minister who is piloting this bill is doing so because the minister in charge of the department is away ill. I am not going to extend my remarks any longer than necessary because I am in favour of the bill.
There is a great need for what this bill sets out to accomplish. Anyone going through that area cannot help but be struck by the destruction that has occurred. I have a report here showing the results of ten years of administration, five years under the federal government and five years under the provincial government. In giving these figures, I do not intend for one moment to censure the provincial government, because their administration of the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains was during the depression yeans when, as everyone knows, revenues were at their lowest ebb. The government of Alberta could not have been expected to provide the same standards of protection that had been provided by the federal government. I have a letter from the department giving the fire losses on the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains at the headwaters of the Saskatchewan river for the years 1925 to 1936. During the period 1925 to 1930 inclusive, when the federal government was administering the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains, the total acreage of timber land destroyed was 58,530 acres, or an average of 11,756 acres a year. During the five years 1931 to 1936 inclusive, when the provincial government was in control- this was at the very depth of the depression when little money was available for these matters-the losses amounted to 235,155 acres, or an average of 47,031 acres a year. That is a terrific loss.
The department was not able to give me any figures following 1936; but if the same rate continued for the ten years since that time, on the basis of 47,031 acres destroyed each year it would mean that another 470,000 acres of timber land could have been destroyed. Whether or not that is the case does not matter for the purposes of my argument, because I want to support the programme the government is now putting forward to assist the Alberta government in preventing the destruction of forests on the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains.
If I had a complaint to make it would be that this bill should have been introduced
Forest Conservation

years ago. As the committee knows, I have advocated such a bill for quite a few years. I am not going to complain over that not having been done, because during that period every dollar was required to prosecute a victorious war. First, because of the depression and, second, because of the war these forests have been destroyed to an extent far beyond what they should have been.
Their importance is hardly estimable. I made a survey last fall in connection with the forests on the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains at the headwaters of the Platte river in the western states. I was informed that the forests on the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains at the headwaters of the Platte river-and this would apply also to the Missouri river-contained approximately one-eighth of the forest wealth of the basin of the Platte. I do not know whether that is the case in Canada, but I imagine it would be safe to say that the forest resources on the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains at the headwaters of the Saskatchewan river would be approximately one-eighth of the wealth and the water resources fifty per cent of the whole basin of the Saskatchewan, which is approximately 149,000 square miles.
The forest wealth on the eastern slope is far greater per square mile or per acre than it is in any other part of the watershed where there is so much in the way of scrub trees, jack pine and trees of little consequence whatever. On the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains there are many fine stands of timber. The importance of the eastern slope to that whole area lies in the fact that in the past it did retain for a long time into the spring and right into the summer vast sheets of ice and snow, and by the retention of that ice and snow the flow in the Saskatchewan river was more even. That, of course, goes without saying. But the reverse effect has followed from the destruction of the forests, and the figures show that the destruction has been great. The result has been that the flow of the Saskatchewan river, as was demonstrated clearly this spring, has been in greater volume than it should have been with the result that it runs off more rapidly and gives little return as it flows down to the sea. In other words, the more that the forests are destroyed by fire, the more rapid is the run-off of the water; and the more the forests are retained, the more permanent the water resources, which are almost priceless to the west, are retained for the benefit of the whole country. So I hope that this legislation will result in more retention of the water resources on the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains.
If I have any comment to make on the bill '*itself I would inquire, first, why the commission is to consist of two appointees of the federal government and one from the provincial government. The whole of this work is 'in Alberta; and, since Alberta is vitally interested, why should not two members of the commission be appointed from Alberta and only one from the federal government? Being on the job there all the time, Alberta might be expected to have a more intense interest in the maintenance of the forests than someone appointed from Ottawa. But I am not going to quarrel with that.
I would ask, further, if the measure is to be considered as a more or less permanent arrangement. I believe that the present limit is twenty-five years, and during the first five years this government is to contribute $6,300,000, plus one half of the cost of maintenance, which is estimated at about $250,000 a year. The federal government will contribute up to $200,000 for maintenance if that should be required, the provincial contribution to maintenance being $125,000 a year. I am not able to say whether that is enough or not. I would hope that the federal government will not stick at the cost of maintenance if it should cost more than $200,000 a year, because the water resources of the Saskatchewan river constitute the most priceless single resource in the west. If the water resources go, everything goes.
It is not mentioned in the bill, but I presume there wrill have to be some arrangement whereby the commission will consult with the P.F.R.A. The P.F.R.A. is a branch of the federal government and it is engaged just now, and I hope will be more so as the years go by, in the conservation of the water resources of the Saskatchewan river watershed. I should therefore think this commission ought to work in close harmony with the P.F.R.A. Under the bill the P.F.R.A. would have no authority, but I have no doubt that the commissioners from Alberta and the dominion government, knowing full well the importance of water conservation, would cooperate together.
The minister will, I hope, tell us something about the programme. Formerly there was some programme for the setting up of fire towers such as we have all through northern Ontario. There would also have to be reservoirs created, although the bill does not mention that, so that water will be available to put out fires either by hose or to be carried by fire truck to put out the fire. I presume that would be part of the capital investment.
I am glad to see that this government is to contribute $6,300,000 for the next five years.

Forest Conservation
I hope that when the five years expire another grant of equal amount will be made for the same purpose because of the vast importance of the preservation of the water resources on the east slope of the Rocky mountains which comes about through the maintenance of the forests. That makes it an investment that is good business. It is money well spent by this government.
I could say a lot more, but perhaps if I sit down the bill will get through more quickly, and I am anxious to see the bill get through. There may be a few amendments to propose; I do not know whether there are or not; but if the western members have amendments that will be helpful, I shall not oppose them. I am grateful to the government as a humble member and as a Canadian long interested in the preservation of the forests on the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains for what the government is doing by this bill. I am anxious to see it in operation.
My Last word is this. While this bill pertains only to the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains, anyone who has travelled through British Columbia must have been horrified times without number as I have been, to contemplate the vast destruction of the forests in that province. One of the most pitiful spectacles one can see is those vast areas along the Fraser and Thompson rivers where formerly thousands and thousands of acres of fine timber grew but which section, through destruction of the forests by fire, is of no more value. So I hope that when the minister finds out, as he will, all the benefits that accrue from reforestation, the preservation of the forests, the conservation of water, the maintenance of the ice and snow which will be the result of reforestation and preservation of the forests, he will bring in another bill to assist British Columbia in the preservation of its forests from destruction bv fire. This is almost too big a job for any single province. I look upon the preservation of the forests of the Rocky mountains on both the eastern slope and the main slope as national business. The headwaters of our great rivers are almost priceless and their maintenance is almost priceless. 1 strongly support this bill.

subtopic: EASTERN SLOPE OF ROCKY MOUNTAINS- AGREEMENT WITH ALEERTA
speechtext:
I am not going to detain the committee very long. I just wish to do something similar to what was done by the hon. member for Davenport who has just taken his seat. I wish to approve the purposes for which this bill is brought before parliament. If there is anything in Canada more important than anything else it is the conservation of our forests. In these circumstances, I believe that the preservation of the forests
and the water resources in this area is more than any one province can undertake by itself. I believe that the government has done the right thing by coming to an agreement with the province whereby the work is to be undertaken by both.
What the hon. member for Davenport said with regard to British Columbia and the destruction and devastation of the forests is true. As a matter of fact he did not put the case as strongly as it should be put. No one can travel by our railways from Alberta through British. Columbia, to the coast without being appalled at the terrible destruction of the finest forest stands in the world. The same is true in a great many cases right across this dominion from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Forests are disappearing. With the disappearance of the forests will soon go the water resources if they are not conserved, and then will come the destruction of the soil through erosion of various kinds.
So far as this group is concerned, this bill will have our full support.

subtopic: EASTERN SLOPE OF ROCKY MOUNTAINS- AGREEMENT WITH ALEERTA
speechtext: Is there any set government policy with regard to giving assistance and protection against forest fires and in furthering conservation methods?

subtopic: EASTERN SLOPE OF ROCKY MOUNTAINS- AGREEMENT WITH ALEERTA
speechtext:
The ownership of the forests carries with, it the responsibility for their protection. That is the usual policy and has been over the years. When the dominion government owned the natural resources of the prairies it bore all the costs of protecting the forests and fighting forest fires. The reason for the government's intervention in this case is, as I said earlier in the debate, that the three provinces are dependent upon the protection of the forests on the east slope of the Rocky mountains. The purpose of the bill is not primarily to protect the forests, although by protecting the forests we achieve the real object of the bill, which is to protect the runoff in the headwaters of the Saskatchewan valley.
The hon. member for Davenport inquired why the commission had two members appointed by the federal government and, one by the provinces. The reason is that the federal government in this case provides all the capital expenditure. The interests of the three provinces must be protected in the carrying out of the. work. It is suggested that the capital expenditure in the amount of $6,300,000 be expended over six years. That is the fixed capital appropriated by this bill. It is provided that the maintenance expense is voted annually by parliament. If the maintenance expense is over $350,000, the province

Forest Conservation
of Alberta pays $125,000. If the maintenance expense is less, the province pays half the maintenance expense. If it is more than $250,000, the money can still be voted by parliament as required, but the provincial contribution is limited to $125,000.
No one can estimate the value of having the forests of the east slope amply protected. Without that, the run-off of the rivers is disturbed and the cost of regulating the How of thie rivers is greatly increased, if not made impossible. Therefore the commission will be made up of at least one forestry engineer of proven capacity to plan the programme of the development of the east slope, and he will be associated with at least one good businessman to see that the government's money is well spent and a representative of the province who, I am sure, will also be competent in the field in which he is appointed.

subtopic: EASTERN SLOPE OF ROCKY MOUNTAINS- AGREEMENT WITH ALEERTA
speechtext: Has there been any negotiating with any other province for a similar work?

subtopic: EASTERN SLOPE OF ROCKY MOUNTAINS- AGREEMENT WITH ALEERTA
speechtext: No other similar situation arises that I know of where the forests of one province protects the headwaters of the rivers of another province.

Section agreed to.
Sections 2 to 5 inclusive agreed to.
On section 6-'Purposes or objects of board.

subtopic: EASTERN SLOPE OF ROCKY MOUNTAINS- AGREEMENT WITH ALEERTA
speechtext: With reference to this section, will there be a regular sub-branch having to do with the destruction of insects and so forth in the forests in addition to the fire prevention branch?

subtopic: EASTERN SLOPE OF ROCKY MOUNTAINS- AGREEMENT WITH ALEERTA
speechtext: All the resources of the government will be available to the commission. At the moment there is a forest insect control board in operation. It happens to be in the Department of Reconstruction and Supply at the present time. It is doing splendid work in experimenting with pests to check insect devastation. The information of the board will be available to this commission. In fact the commission can, of course, call on all the resources of the federal government which may be required to enable it to carry out its work efficiently.

Section agreed to.
Sections 7 to 10 inclusive agreed to.

subtopic: ADJUSTMENT OP BOUNDARIES, ADDITIONS, ETC.

speechtext: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Acting Minister of Mines and Resources) moved the second reading of Bill No. 365, respecting certain national parks and to amend the National Parks Act.

subtopic: ADJUSTMENT OP BOUNDARIES, ADDITIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Will the minister explain the bill?

subtopic: ADJUSTMENT OP BOUNDARIES, ADDITIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since this bill, if enacted, will divest the crown of areas of land in certain of the national parks, the title to which is at present in the crown, His Excellency the Governor General wasrinformed in respect thereto and has given his consent to the consideration of the bill.
Briefly, the purpose of this bill is:
(1)	To add to Fort Beausejour historic park two small parcels totalling a little more than four acres of historic ground.
(2)	To withdraw from Riding Mountain national park a marginal 640 acres of land which is being exchanged with the owner of a similar area of land well inside the park which is of greater value for park purposes and which will be included in the park by this legislation.
(3)	To add to Elk Island national park approximately twenty-four square miles of territory immediately south of the park which is required to protect the health and welfare of the buffalo herd.
(4)	To withdraw from Prince Albert national park 373 square miles of territory which is not suitable for park purposes and which is needed for a dominion-provincial fur conservation scheme which will benefit the Indians, half-breeds and other residents leading the hunting life.
(5)	To withdraw from Waterton lakes national park sixteen square miles of territory on the east end that is not suitable for national park development, but is actually required for grazing and timber by nearby settlers.
(6)	To abolish Nemiskam park near Foremost and Buffalo national park near Wain-wright as these areas are no longer required for park purposes.
(7)	To vest in the governor general in council the additional power to grant leases of lots in subdivisions for the purposes of residence during summer months only and to provide for extensions and changes in existing townsites and subdivisions.
(8)	To authorize agreements with any province in which a national park is situated

National Parks
extending to park residents social services which are supplied by that province to persons resident outside of the park.
The explanations given in the bill are, I believe, quite adequate. However, for the information of the committee, I should like to explain more fully some of the changes being made in regard to certain parks.
Hon. members will recall that at the 1941 session a bill was introduced to amend the boundaries of Prince Albert national park, and that bill was withdrawn because of the opposition raised at that time. The war was then in progress, and the matter was not of sufficient importance to engage too much of the time of the house.
Section 3 of the present bill now asks that the same areas be removed from the park and be declared to be no longer required for park purposes. I might say that this park was created in 1927 prior to the transfer of the resources and was originally known as the Sturgeon forest reserve. The area is 1,869 square miles. It is proposed to remove three areas containing approximately 376 square miles; the area remaining in the park being approximately 1,493 square miles.
Parcel No. 1 containing 340 square miles is located on the northeast side of the park and is unsuitable for park purposes. There are no lakes of outstanding value; the ground is very low and full of muskegs, and there is no fishing in any of the small lakes. Vertical aerial photographs of the area were taken in 1946, and later the area was cruised. The timber resources are very limited. The total amount of the merchantable coniferous saw timber is estimated at 1,577,500 feet board measure of white spruce located in six separate blocks, some of which are in insufficient quantities to make an economical operation feasible. The remainder of the area does not at present contain any timber of sawlog size, although there are small quantities of jack pine ties and poplar cordwood. Generally the area is unattractive. On the other hand, it surrounds the Montreal lake Indian reserve and is suitable for incorporation in the fur conservation programme that has beem agreed upon between the dominion and the province for northern Saskatchewan.

The provincial government has agreed that when the area is deleted, from the park it will be included in the scheme which will permit the Indians to have equal trapping rights with the native population under the conditions of the agreement.
I should add that this reason for removing the parcel did not exist when the matter was before the house some years ago. I do not wish to take up time to discuss the joint fur conservation programme except to say that it is hoped it will be of great benefit to the trapping Indians in Saskatchewan. The inclusion of this parcel will facilitate the plans being made in that section of the country.
Parcel No. 2 comprises approximately ten square miles and is located on the southeast corner of the park. It is of no particular value to the park and is required as an addition to the adjacent Little Red River Indian reserve 106A. It is an area which juts out from the main block and adds unnecessarily to the length of the park boundary. When the land is reverted to the province it will then be transferred to the dominion to be added to the Indian reserve.
Parcel No. 3 contains approximately twenty-six square miles. It is located in the southwest corner of the park and is of no value for park purposes. On the other hand, it is suitable for agriculture. Like parcel No. 2, it lengthens the boundaries of the park and thereby increases the cost of administration. Apart from a certain portion of the park highway, approximately five miles, running through it and the telephone lines, there are no other park improvements situated in it.
In reference to the abolition of Buffalo park at Wainwright, as most members are aware the buffalo herd at this park was disposed of in the years 1939 and 1940. A number of the healthy animals were transferred to Elk island and the remainder slaughtered. At the present time there are approximately 1,200 animals in good condition at Elk island park. An arrangement has been made with the province to increase the area of this park by adding approximately 23-6 square miles from the Cooking lake reserve immediately adjacent; this is being transferred to the dominion and is being incorporated in the park by section 2, paragraph (c) of this bill. With the added area, which is very suitable for pasture, there will be sufficient land to maintain the present number of animals and to ensure for all time the preservation of this species.
